Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO - Report of First War Patrol.

(A) PROLOGUE

This ship was placed in commission at the U.S. Navy Yard, Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on 6 November 1943. Training was commenced 29 November 1943 in the Portsmouth, Newport, New London area. During the period 29 November 1943 to 15 January 1944 conducted the following: boat trials, practice approaches, 6-day practice patrol, fired contract torpedo trials, dock and sound tested, fired 3 exercise torpedoes, test fired all guns, calibrated pitometer log, in drydock a total of 11 days undergoing repairs to propeller shaft bearings.

Departed New London, Connecticut on 15 January 1944. Made transit of Panama Canal on 24 January 1944. In Balboa, Canal Zone area from 26 January to 29 January 1944 for minor repairs and sound tests. Arrived Pearl Harbor, T.H. on 14 February 1944. Base repairs from 14 February 1944 to 22 February 1944 including a 5-day period in ARD #1 drydock for repairs to propeller shaft bearings. Commenced final training 23 February 1944. Conducted torpedo approaches, night dummy motor runs, fired 4 exercise torpedoes, was sound tested and received indoctrination depth charging.

On 6 March 1944 in accordance with orders of ComSubPac, Lieutenant Commander Paul E. Summers, U. S. Navy, relieved Lieutenant Commander Charles B. Jackson, Jr., U.S. Navy, as commanding officer. Commenced additional training period of 6 days for new commanding officer. Made practice approaches, night and day radar rehearsal runs, and fired 6 exercise torpedoes.

Major work accomplished in Pearl Harbor Area was as follows:

(1) Renewed woods and rebored inboard bearings on both propeller shafts.

(2) Completed installations for charging and ventilating Mk. 18 torpedoes in both torpedo rooms.

(3) Installed the following: Mark Island type nickel eliminator for battery water; baffle plate in #1 M.B.T. to decrease flooding time; RSN-3 Radio receiver; voice modulation equipment for TBL-7 radio transmitter; C10 radar detector; IFF radio equipment; variable speed training power for SJ radar mast.

(4) The ship was painted with dark gray camouflage color on vertical surfaces.

Training was completed on 12 March 1944 and loading completed on 14 March 1944, with 16 MK. 14, MOD. 3A torpedoes in forward torpedo room and 8 MK. 18 torpedoes in after torpedo room.

Subject: U.S.S. ATANITO - Report of First War Patrol.

1356 (K)Set up looks fairly good, came left to 110° for about 75° starboard track on leading target. The escort is crossing over toward us from port to starboard bow of target. A second look disclosed a small mast well astern and to the starboard of second ship in column. Probably another escort.
1330 (K)With track of about 75° starboard, zero gyro angle and torpedo run of about 1400 yards, up periscope for final check on set-up, disclosing the following: leading escort was heading almost directly for us at range of less than 500 yards, leading target was zigging away to the left, with smoke billowing from his stack. And at
1331 (K)Received one depth charge; not close. Decided to go deep and try to run under target and get on other side of formation for a possible attack on second target, as it would have been wasting torpedoes, had I let go at the leading target with the set-up changing so rapidly and with target heading away. Very puzzled over the fact that the escort was able to pick me up, in that I was very cautious in the amount of periscope exposed and the duration of my exposure was held to a minimum. Think perhaps he may have picked up air noise while we were making the tubes ready, else he is very good at echo ranging.
1345 (K)Started up to periscope depth. Sound reported escort astern, with second target on our port quarter.
1348 (K)Received 2 depth charges fairly close to starboard and above. Went deep.
1403 - 1405 (K)Received a string of 5 depth charges varying in depth from about 150 to 600 feet, all very close with two straddles. During this interval we heard the screws of one escort through our hull, and the sound man distinctly made out a definite ping similar to a fathometer as the escort passed over us and let go his charges. This string of 5 depth charges caused considerable damage and shaking up of the boat as evidenced by inspections later. Damages are listed under Major Defects and Damages.
1406 (K)We can definitely hear two escorts now pinging on us.
1407 - 1600 (K)Continued evasive tactics at deep submergence with both escorts coming in and going out intermittently. We have been unable to locate a definite gradient at any depth thus far.
1600 (K)Sound reported high speed screws moving out, so started up slowly to periscope depth. Trim very heavy at present, but think it unwise to use trim pump until I take a look.

0600 (K)Dived to routine torpedoes forward and aft.

Upon pulling torpedoes forward, we found the following: torpedo in #2 tube had flooded exploder; torpedoes in tubes #5 and #6 had flooded after bodies, other torpedoes were dry.

All torpedoes forward were made ready for firing yesterday and the pressure in the tubes of those torpedoes which were flooded was never greater than 20 to 25 lbs. Cannot explain the fact of their flooding except that the shock from the depth charging may have been enough to break the exhaust valve seals. In order to properly routine the flooded after bodies on torpedoes in #5 and #6 tubes, will have to submerge again tomorrow to complete the job.

Inspection of the torpedo s in the after tubes disclosed that the shock from yesterday's depth charging had put two cracks in a section of the battery cells of one Mk. 18 torpedo.

Subject: U.S.S. TARANTO - Report of First War Patrol.

Stationed the radar tracking party and commenced tracking. Found convoy to consist of two large ships with 4 possible escorts: one escort ahead, one on either flank and one astern. The two large ships seem to be in column, zig-zagging on base course about 195° T., with a speed of 9 knots.

0400 (K)Commenced end around.
0407 (K)Observed both targets to be smoking at frequent intervals.
0503 (K)First track of dawn. True bearing of convoy 275° T., range 10,500 yards. Will have to open out and try to get ahead for a daylight attack.

Tracked the two targets out to 34,000 yards with radar, so they are evidently very large AK's.

0714 (K)In position ahead of convoy, range about 35,000 yards. Dived. Went deep to find an injection temperature gradient but could find none down to 400 feet.
0925 (K)At depth of 50 feet, maintaining periscope and sound watch.
1020 (K)Sound picked up echo-ranging bearing about 340° T.
1030 (K)Periscope sighted smoke bearing 342° T. Commenced approach. As convoy came in sight, made out the following: two large 7000 ton freighters (similar to TUYAMA MARU and TOKAI MARU), Force 208 and 226 respectively of ONI 208-J) in column, zig-zagging similarly, closely using short zigs, with a roving destroyer screen on either flank of target group, and a similar destroyer using constant helm about 1500-3000 yards ahead of target group, plus a subcheaser astern of targets. All 3 destroyers were similar to FUBUKI type.
1128 (K)With target group dead ahead, angle on bow zero and with leading destroyer at range of about 5,000 yards, went to 100 feet to pass underneath this screen, and knock clear, to come right for a 90 track, stern shot at leading target. However once at this depth and after coming right for a stern shot, the leading destroyer dropped back on the port bow of leading target, making two screens on this side. According to sound, both of these DD's were moving back and forth ahead and astern of us, and I was gradually opening out from the track. So at --
1144 (K)With one DD still between us and the targets, decided to come left for a bow shot on second freighter in column.
1150 (K)At periscope depth, convoy had zigged away presenting about 150° angle on the bow with a range greater than 6,000 yards.

Decided to wait until range opened out sufficiently to surface and then make an end around and get in an attack after dark.

11 April 1944

0015 (K) Destroyer screws going away.
0043 (K) Surfaced. All clear. After careful consideration of the following casualties, decided it would be wise to pull clear and try to effect repairs rather than pursue convoy: (1) Outboard air induction piping completely flooded. (2) Both sound head training motors grounded out. (3) A flooded MJ. 18 torpedo in #9 torpedo tube, having been subjected to sea pressure while evading - due to leaky outer door gasket.
0300 (K) Sent contact report on 450 hoping HARDER will receive it; also sent PAMPANITO second dispatch to Comsubpac. Since I did not see our target sink, I am hoping HARDER will make contact with same convoy, and verify my belief that the target we hit did sink and was missing from convoy.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO - Report of First War Patrol.

0603 (K)Dived. Patrolling north covering Guam-Palau route.
Located several leaks today in flange fittings of outboard air induction piping. Will try to repair these tonight.
Unable to pull MK. 18 torpedo from #9 tube. Will investigate that further.
1845 (K)Surfaced. Commenced work on leaky flanges to outboard air induction piping. Found loose bolts on several flanges. Tightened these. Will test this again tomorrow to see if we did any good in stopping leaks.
By use of a "Jary Rig" we finally pulled the MK. 18 torpedo from #9 tube. The entire torpedo was completely flooded, with warhead casing "Dished in" in several places; battery cells cracked, deformed and completely flooded.
Battery cells are beyond salvaging, so threw them overboard. Other parts of torpedo will be properly cleaned up and preserved as best possible and retained on board.
The armatures and field coils of both sound head training motors have zero grounds and open circuits. So will be unable to use them the remainder of patrol. However, have hopes of trying our lathe motor as a sound head training motor. It may work.

Yap Island

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS383) - Report of first

1. The first war patrol of the PAMPANITO covered a
period of fifty-five days, of which thirty were spent in the
assigned area and on Special Lifeguard Mission. The patrol
was terminated because of fuel limitations.

2. Only two contacts worthy of torpedo fire were
made.

Contact 1 - Consisted of two small AKs of about 4,000 tons
zigging radically with one escort, Chidori type, ranging ahead
and one escort ranging astern. A submerged day periscope ap-
proach was made and a good firing position obtained. On rais-
ing periscope for final check the Chidori was observed less
than 500 yards range headed directly for submarine. Depth
charging forced the submarine to evade at deep submergence.
Subsequent pursuit was made but contact was not regained.

Attack 1 - Consisted of two 7,000 ton AKs with three Fubuki
type destroyer escorts, one constant-helming ahead of the
convoy 1,500 to 3,000 yards and one on either flank. A submerged
day periscope approach was made but good firing position was not
attained because of alert escorts and evasive measures taken by
convoy. An end-around was made during the night and a submerged
night radar approach begun from ahead. Four bow torpedoes fired,
range 2,400 yards, on leading target, 200 percent target cover-
age. Two timed hits, one of which was a very violent explosion.
The target's screws were reported stopped by sound. The remain-
ing two bow torpedoes were fired at one of the escorts, range
2,400 yards. No hits were heard or observed. Depth charging
forced the submarine to deep submergence.
Damage assessment - One AK, 7,000 tons, damage.

3. Thirty four air contacts were made which gave the
PAMPANITO considerable training in diving the boat. The skill
manifested by the crew in the repair of casualties sustained as

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO - Report of Second War Patrol.

(A) PROLOGUE

Arrived Submarine Base, Pearl Harbor, T.H. from First War Patrol on 8 May 1944 for normal refit by Submarine Base and Submarine Division 42 Relief Crew. Drydocked in ARD #1 from 9 to 12 May 1944. Major work items accomplished during refit were:

(1) Conversion of #4 MBT to FBT.
(2) Rearrangement of officer' country with installation of two additional bunks.
(3) Replacement of rubber flange gaskets in main induction piping in superstructure with Consolco gaskets.
(4) Renewed gaskets and realigned all outer torpedo tube doors while in drydock.
(5) Installation of DRT in conning tower.
(6) Installation of circulating water pump for cooling engines while submerged.
(7) Installation of two (2) high pressure globe stop valves in engine room circulating salt water system.
(8) Removal of CUD and installation of APR.
(9) Installation of VHF receiver and transmitter.

Underway sound tests and training exercises were conducted 27 - 31 May 1944. Loading accomplished 1 - 2 June. One day extension granted for grinding in leaky sea valves and installation of 2 high pressure globe stop valves in main engine circulating salt water system.

Machinist James Samuel Heist, USN was detached and Lieutenant (jg) Ted Neir Swain, USN, reported aboard. Readiness for sea 3 June 1944.

(B) NARRATIVE

3 June 1944

1330 (VW)Underway from Pearl Harbor, T.H. enroute patrol area via Midway in accordance with Comsaskfor Seventeen Operation Order 191-44 of 1 June 1944.
1530 (VW)Made deep test dive. Results: flooded SJ radar mast; engine salt water sea valves still leaking; both periscopes extremely rough in train; considerable noise and vibration around periscope shears.
1626 (VW)Surfaced. Drained SJ Radar Mast, flushed out with fresh water, dried with air and installed new face plate gasket on parabola housing. Subsequent tests of SJ radar and lobing appeared to be satisfactory. Will have it further checked in Midway.
2000 (VW)Released escort, PC-485; proceeding independently.

The weather was excellent enroute from Midway until about 300 miles east of NANPO SHOTO when we encountered the edge of a typhoon, with mountainous seas, strong wind and a dropping barometer plus frequent heavy rain squalls. After passing north of TOAI SHIMA, the seas and wind moderated, but the uninterred squally weather for the next 24 hours.

The weather in the areas south of Japan was usually mild with frequent rain squalls of short duration and relatively calm and glassy-smooth seas. Visibility conditions varied from fair to poor, mainly due to the hazy conditions that seem to persist with a smooth sea in this area.

Weather enroute to Midway from NANPO SHOTO was in general excellent with light swells and good visibility.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS383) - Report of war Patrol Number TWO,
Comments on.

1. The second war patrol of the U.S.S. PAMPANITO was in areas
off the Japanese empire. Thirty-two days were spent in the areas during
which period the PAMPANITO made seven contacts with surface ships worthy
of torpedo attack, but on only one was she able to close within torpedo
range. Three torpedoes were fired on this attack and one hit was heard in
a 5100 ton freighter. Area coverage was good in spite of heavy surface
and air patrol. Surface patrol was strong off the 100 fathom curve, and
caused the PAMPANITO considerable trouble when closing the Coast. Strong
currents in these coastal areas made navigation difficult and submerged
patrol transits.

2. ATTACK NUMBER ONE.

This was a periscope attack on July 6th on a convoy consist-
ing of two medium AK's and one small AC with three escorts. Three Mark
18-1 torpedoes were fired from the stern tubes at one of the escorts, an
Otari type torpedo boat, but the target believed hit was a 5100 ton AK
similar to the Toyokawa Maru class. All three torpedoes were fired with a
2° divergent spread on tracks between 60°s and 67° respectively. Depth settings
were eight feet on numbers 7 and 8 tubes and 10 feet on number 9 tube.
One torpedo explosion was heard about six and one-half minutes after firing
the first torpedo. Sound tracked the torpedoes to the screws of a ship
which stopped after the explosion. Breaking-up noises and popping noises
were heard for forty-five minutes after the explosion. A depth charge attack
prevented making an observation until an hour and a quarter after firing.
At this time only the torpedo boat and a float plane were in sight circling
the area in which the ship was last seen and heard. The length of the tor-
pedo run is exceptionally long for a Mark 18-1 torpedo and coincides very
closely with the time for an end of run explosion. However, since the
Commanding Officer insists that he heard the torpedo hit a ship and the
ship screws stopped, after which breaking-up noises were heard it is be-
lieved that the ship was either sunk or damaged.

Subject: U. S. S. PAMPANITO - Report of Third War Patrol

A) PROLOGUE

Arrived Submarine Base, Midway Island, T.H. from Second War Patrol on 23 July 1944 for normal refit by U.S.S. PROTEUS and Submarine Division 262 Relief Crew. Stood in ARD-8 from 3 to 5 August 1944. Major work items accomplished during refit were:

1. Removed gaskets in conning tower hatch, main induction hull valve and No. 1 flood valve in No. 4A Fuel Ballast Tank.

(2) Renewed all main motor brushes with new "USN" type.

(3) Installed radio key in SJ radar circuit for communications.

(4) Completed installing MK. 18 charging equipment in forward torpedo room.

Underway sound tests conducted 8 August 1944. Underway training exercises conducted 9 to 14 August 1944. Loading accomplished 14-15 August 1944. On 12 August 1944, Lieutenant (jg) William L. Bruckart, D-V(RS), USNR was detached and Lieutenant(jg) Richard J. Sherlock, D-V(RS), USNR reported on board for duty. On 15 August 1944, Ensign Percy E. Pike, USN, was detached because of illness and Ensign Charles K. Bartholomew, D-V(S), USNR reported on board for duty on 16 August 1944. Readiness for sea on 15 August 1944. Two day delay due to a casualty to #4 main motor. A section of the compensating winding shorted across the series field winding resulting in burned insulation, burned brushes, and much loose carbon scattered throughout the motor; cause not definitely determined. The damage was repaired by the tender on 15-16 August 1944. Underway for 3rd War Patrol on 17 August 1944.

shouting but we couldn't understand what they were saying, except made out words "Pick us up please". Called rescue party on deck and took them off the raft. There were about fifteen (15) British and Australian Prisoners of War survivors on this raft from a ship sunk the night of 11-12 September 1944. We learned they were enroute from SINGAPORE to FORMOSA and they there were over thirteen hundred on the sunken ship.

As men were received on board, we stripped them and removed most of the heavy coating of oil and muck. We cleared the after torpedo room and passed them below as quickly as possible. Gave all men a piece of cloth moistened with water to suck on. All of them were exhausted after four days on the raft and three years imprisonment. Many had lashed themselves to their makeshift rafts, which were slick with grease; and had nothing but life belts with them. All showed signs of pellagra, beri-beri, immersion, salt water sores, ringworm, malaria, etc. All were very thin and showed the results of undernourishment. Some were in very bad shape, but with the excitement of rescue they came alongside with cheers for the Yanks and many a curse for the Nips. It was quite a struggle to keep them on the raft while we took them off one by one. They could not manage to secure a line to the raft, so we sent men over the side who did the job. The survivors came tumbling aboard and then collapsed with strength almost gone. A pitiful sight none of us will ever forget. All hands turned to with a will and the men were cared for as rapidly as possible.

Subject:

U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS323) - Report of THIRD War Patrol.

1. The third war patrol of PAMPANITO, as a member of a coordinated attack group which also included U.S.S. GROWLER (Lieutenant Commander T.B. OAKLEY J.T.O.) and U.S.S. SEA LION, was brief, spectacular and effective. Of forty-two (42) days on patrol seventeen (17) were spent in the assigned area, LUZON STRAITS and SOUTH CHINA SEAS.

2. The only contact worthy of torpedo fire was encountered on 12 September. The group made radar contact with a large convoy at 0130. While maneuvering for position PAMPANITO observed attacks by GROWLER at 0155 and SEA LION at 0527. Further action on the part of the enemy made a long day light chase necessary. Air cover forced PAMPANITO to submerge at 1359 and again at 1516. As a consequence contact was lost at a very critical moment in view of the enemy's established habit of making a radical alteration of base course at dusk. However, thoughtful estimate of enemy's probably movement resulted in contact being established at 2106. At this time the remnant of the convoy consisted of one large transport, two large and one medium cargo ships and an undetermined number of escorts.

3. PAMPANITO maneuvered to obtain a position which afforded favorable track angles with moderate torpedo run and small gyro angles and attacked all principal ships with nine torpedoes. Hits were observed in three of the targets and a timed hit was heard but not seen in the fourth. The large transport and one large cargo ship were seen to sink. The second large cargo ship caught fire and was observed, abandoned and still burning on 14 September.

4. After reloading PAMPANITO closed the scene of action and made radar contact with two widely separated targets. One of these, identified as an escort, was unsuccessfully attacked with three torpedoes from a firing position that cannot be called the best. Torpedo run was nearly extreme, and the spread used was excessive. It is probable that these factors rather than faulty depth performance caused the miss.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO - Report of Fourth War Patrol.

(A) PROLOGUE

Arrived Submarine Base, Pearl Harbor, T.H. from Third War Patrol on 28 September 1944 for normal refit by Submarine Base, Pearl Harbor, T.H. and Submarine Division 281 Relief Crew. Major jobs accomplished were: Overhaul of three main and the auxiliary engines; installation of Mark 8 TBT's; replacement of all type SAE 1045 USN motor brushes with old type SAE 1045; installation of Navy type VHF; new slotted SJ reflector; APR with oscilloscope; Gould trim pump; new all steel rectangle gasket hatches in all positions except forward torpedo room, gun trunk and conning tower (hatches not available for these three openings).

On 7 October 1944, Captain FRANK W. FENNO, JR., USN. relieved Commander PAUL E. SUMMERS, USN, as Commanding Officer. Training period 17 to 25 October 1944. Loading 26-27 October 1944. Readiness for sea on 28 October 1944.

PAMPANITO group commander. Set course for Midway at two engine speed. Conducted dives, radar tracking, general and fire control drills, and communication exercises for wolf pack while enroute. Speed 14½ knots (2 main engines) enroute.

It was not until late that night that it was realized SEACAT and SEARAVEN were both in contact with SEARAVEN's crippled AO and that the SEACAT's 12 knot target had slowed to four knots. Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS383) - Report of War Patrol No. Four.

1. During the fourth war patrol of the PAMPANITO the Commanding Officer, Captain F. W. FENNO, U.S. Navy acted as commander of a coordinated search and attack group operating off Hainan. During the patrol three torpedo attacks were made, all with Mark 18 torpedoes.

2. Attack No. 1 was made on 1 November 1944 on a convoy consisting of two large freighters and an escort. Six bow tubes were fired at the leading freighter in a night surface radar attack, from good position. Two hits were observed which finished off this ship. The PAMPANITO swung and fired four stern shots at the second freighter. One hit was heard which caused a small fire. Torpedoes used incomplete coverage of 600 feet and 425 feet respectively. The second freighter was subsequently attacked by another submarine of the pack but the attack was unsuccessful and the freighter and escort made for the coast.

3. Attack No. 2 on 30 November was a periscope attack at dawn after a five hour end around in bright moonlight against a high speed convoy of four ships and three escorts. A chance in base course put the PAMPANITO well off the track and an estimated 4000 yard range had to be accepted. Three torpedoes were fired at the leading ship, and three at the second ship in column, both medium tankers. Spread used covered 900 feet in both cases. There were no visible results of the attack, but five explosions were heard which could have been hits at extreme range or end of run explosions.

4. Attack No. 3 on 3 December was a coordinated attack on a convoy of 1 merchantman, one convoy was successfully attacked by other submarines of the pack during the night. PAMPANITO tracked for one and one half hours and made a periscope attack at dawn. The four after tubes were fired at a large tanker. The PAMPANITO forced deep by escorts before the bow tubes could be brought to bear and before results of the attack could be observed. Again explosions were heard which could have been hits at extreme range or end of run explosions. This attack was made in very heavy seas, but attack No. 2 was made in a dead calm sea. In attack No. 3 the range was estimated as 3960 yards, 45° track, spread covered 900 feet.

5. The patrol was conducted on the surface. The SD radar was used continuously and no air craft bombing was experienced, although fifty contacts were made, forcing the PARCHE down forty-two times, four of these dives being at night. Five floating mines were sighted off Hainan. Heavy seas prevented destruction of these by gun fire. The information on interception of enemy radar transmission is complete and is of great value.

6. The PARCHE returned in good material condition. A normal refit will be conducted by Sub Submarine and Submarine Division 121 Relief Crew. The excellent performance of the electronic gear is worthy of note. This was a long patrol, both in time and mileage. In sixty-three days PARCHE steamed 16,406 miles.

7. The Squadron Commander welcomes the PARCHE and congratulates the Commanding Officer, officers and men on a fine patrol. This is Captain Ramage's fourth submarine command during the war and even though this patrol was long and arduous due to heavy weather, the morale and enthusiasm of the crew of the PARCHE was at the high standard we have come to expect of Captain Ramage's commands.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS395) - Report of Fourth War
Patrol - Comments on.

1. The Fourth War Patrol of the PAMPANITO was conducted
in Commander Submarines Pacific Areas of interest, as a member
of a coordinated search and attack group consisting of PAMPANITO
(CTC), SEALION and PIPEFISH.

2. PAMPANITO is the fourth submarine to be commanded
in this war by Captain P. E. SUMMERS and this patrol was conducted
in the well planned and effective manner which has characterized
all of this veteran submarine commander's previous patrols. After
observing the approach tactics throughout three attacks on this
Area, the Commanding Officer decided to fully exploit the advantages
of surface patrol during daylight. Although fifty aircraft contacts
were made and PAMPANITO was forced down forty two times, the
prevailing high state of training and its resulting alertness
prevented her from being bombed a single time.

3. The first attack on the eighteenth of November, was
a night radar attack on a three ship convoy which was not zig-
zagging. Six bow and four stern tubes were fired and two hits were
observed to sink one ship and one hit was observed to damage
another. The second attack was made on a freighter during bright
moonlight which necessitated a submerged periscope approach. Six
torpedoes were fired at two targets, but no hits were observed.
The third attack, on 9 December was conducted submerged in very
rough seas upon a convoy which consisted of four ships and several
escorts. The four stern tubes were fired at a range 20 and one hit
damaged the target.

4. All of the assessed damage took place in Areas under
the Operational Control of Commander Submarines Pacific Fleet.

Subject: U.S.S. PALPALITO - Report of Fifth War Patrol.

(I) PROLOG

PALPALITO arrived North Wharf, Fremantle, Western Australia, 30 December 1944 from Fourth War Patrol. Assigned to Submarine Division 161 and Submarine Squadron 16 for refit and availability to put forth Repair Unit, Navy #137 for refit. The major work items accomplished during refit were: the elimination of the torpedo tube shutters and shutter lids: the installation of deodor hatches in the after battery after torpedo room and after torpedo room hatches; and the addition of two 20 mm gun shields on the after 20 M/m gun.

Commander KING, L. STIRLING, USN, with seal Captain FRANK G. FENNO, Jr., USN as Commanding Officer on 2 January 1945. Lieutenant Commander LANDON L. DAVIS, Jr., USN, was relieved as Executive Officer by Lieutenant (T) Commander IRWIN S. DAVIS. The new additional senior board member of the crew is ARTHUR T. McBRIDE, USN, who relieved ensign withdrawn. Ensign ARTHUR WILLIAM J. BUSH, USNR, reported on board as Fourth Watch Officer. Departed on 15 January 1945 and having briefed D. A. having duly reported on board for duty on 14 January 1945.

The refit was completed 14 January 1945. Seven days post repair and training during which were reported. in the ready magazine. Fired 4" gun, and fired torpedo exercise torpedoes; were followed by two days loading. Readiness for sea on 23 January 1945.

Subject: U.S.S. SEALION - Report of Fifth War Patrol.

NARRATIVE (Continued)

0029 (I) Had just about checked off three misses when the first torpedo hit and simultaneously the ship disintegrated with the bow going one way, the stern in the opposite direction and part of the ship going straight up. Judging from the intense flames and explosions, this ship was evidently loaded with aviation gasoline. One second we'd close our eyes, the sure to share in the effects of the explosions. The second torpedo probably hit whatever was left to hit. The whole area looked like a Fourth of July celebration we all slightly naked in all this starlight. Escort on starboard quarter and checked firing at us and placed several rounds just over the bridge before we could pull clear on all four main engines. For the next twenty minutes one violent explosion followed another as ship was torn to pieces. The stern sank and the bow set on the finishing touch by exploding beautifully and in technicolor.

0041 (I) All clear of escort.

0200 (H) Sent in ULTRA third to CTF 71.

0454 (H) Made rendezvous with GUAVINA and transmitted bearing and mail for INDO on hand. Sub course south.

0519 (H) Plane contact 19 miles (Plane Contact #6). Dived. Went down slowly when one EB-2 and 2D AFT would not open in normal power and had to be opened by hand; fortunately no homing.

1000 (I) After checking operation of all vents, surfaced.

1318 (H) Plane sighted from bridge (Plane Contact #7) so dived.

1345 (H) Surfaced; all clear.

0011 (I) Received message ordering us to reverse course and head for southeast corner B - 3 and await further orders.

1604 (H) Made trim dive.

1620 (H) Surfaced.

Enroute southeast corner Area B-3.

11 February 1945

1310 (I) Received message to proceed to Subic Bay, Philippine Islands for refit.

ATTACK DATA

U.S.S. PARCHE (SS384) TORPEDO ATTACK NO. 1 PATROL NO. 5

Time - 2157(H). Date - 6 February 1945. Lat. - 06° 29' N. Long. - 106° 11.5' E.

Target Data - Damage Inflicted

Description - At 1653 (H) smoke was sighted by the high periscope and tracking determined it was heading north. Set course to starboard to gain a favorable position for a night approach. The smoke proved to be from one ship of a convoy consisting of the following ships: 1 large AK or AP; 1 large AO or AK; 1 medium small burning AK and 1 escort. One of the escorts appeared to be a SHIOCHI type destroyer escort and the others were PC type patrol vessels. The three ships in the convoy were in a line of bearing of about 255° and 1600 yards apart. The large AK or AP was the leading ship, the large AK or AO was the second ship and the medium AK was the third ship. One escort was ahead of the formation, one escort on either flank and escort astern. The night was clear but the moon had not risen. It was too dark for a periscope attack and too light for a close range surface attack.

Ship Sunk - 3 large AK or AP - 7900 tons (AU).

Damage - Determined by - Two torpedo hits were observed from the bridge in the leading ship; one near the stern and the other just aft of amidships superstructure. The ship was then seen to go down by the stern and two escorts closed on this ship. The radar pip decreased in intensity until it disappeared. The remaining pips were tracked for about 30 minutes, but the two escorts (identified by a PIT) were observed by radar to be milling around the same general vicinity apparently picking up survivors. Upon the completion of the third attack we returned to this position and the two escorts were still milling around but there were no signs of the large ship.

Target Course - 040° T. Target Speed - 8 Knots. Target Range - 4300 Yards.

134:
Subject: U.S.S. TILEFISH - Report of Fifth War Patrol.

(D) MINES

One floating mine was sighted in Lat. 06° 07.7' N., Long. 103° 55.8' E. It was spherical in shape, about four feet in diameter, and had three horns. Mine was sunk by rifle fire but mine would not sink or explode.

(E) ANTI-SUBMARINE MEASURES AND EVASION TACTICS

First convoy and zig-zagging during daylight - twin engine bomber. After first attack escorts fired guns in all directions. Several depth charges were also dropped. On second run third attacks escorts gave chase. On fourth attack we were not sighted. On fifth attack the exploding tanker lighted the whole area thus exposed put our shot just over our bridge, and sprayed ping death charges.

(F) MAJOR DEFECTS AND DAMAGE

No incidents - The auxiliary converter has been a source round on the compensating fluid since leaving for patrol. Since the end of this war, the converter has never run too erature which have to be lifted to remove the coil attempt was made to remove the ground by cleaning and painting with glyptol with the coil in place. The attempt was not successful.

A main engine developed blow holes in the cylinder liner under the seat of the air start actuator. These blow holes were filled with silver liner evidently had expanded from the heat of the exhaust gases and cracked the water jacket. Water-glands have cracked water jackets. These pockets were made and fitted to the glands to prevent excessive water loss. A main engine still evaporates at full load and will require having all water lines and all lines pulled out and inspected.

The torpedo connection to the linkage of #2 outboard exhaust valve to the hydraulic power piston parted. The remaining piece of the toggle was drilled, threaded and a stud made to hold the linkage together.

Torpedo and Gunnery - The 40 MM gun installed before the start of this run was in such a condition that it could not be leveled. The feed pawls were installed in the step pawl holder and the step pawls in the feed pawl holder. Thus the first cartridge could not go locker over the first feed pawl due to the fact that the step pawl holder has no groove for the feed pawl to ride in.

(G) RADIO

No defects were experienced in radio equipment. On 29 and 30 January 1945 at 0100 zebra there was intentional jamming of the time tick.

(H) RADAR

SJ-1 Radar - The performance of the SJ-1 was not as satisfactory this run as on previous patrols. This seems to be a result of changing magnetrons during our last refit. The rin was only 4000 yards with the new magnetrons as compared to 5600 yards with the old ones. By trying our spares, one was found that increased the ring to 5600 yards but as yet a good range check has not been made.

SJ-4 Radar - The SJ performance was good throughout this run. The equipment operated exceptionally in rain areas in the radio receiver which should be eliminated during the next refit.

I.F.F. - The APR and MN operating is satisfactory.

(H) SOUND GEAR AND SOUND CONDITIONS

Time submerged this patrol was so small, there are no remarks about sound conditions.

(J) DENSITY LAYERS

The few days spent in the area and the scarcity of dives gave opportunity for only three bathythermograph card readings. Each card indicated a 1 to 1½ degree negative gradient beginning at approximately 50 feet below the surface and extending to a probable 60 feet. Since the depth of water in this area is considered limited to approximately 30 fathoms no dives deeper than 140 feet keel depth were made.

(K) HEALTH, FOOD AND HABITABILITY

The general health of the officers and men was excellent throughout this patrol.

The food was well prepared, but not up to the usual standards because of the inability to obtain all the desired items. The meat obtainable was below standard.

The increased number of men on board made living conditions crowded but this was more than offset by ease of watch standing. With present stills, water restrictions was necessary to have water at the end of a long patrol.

(L) PERSONNEL

The performance of duty of all hands was highly satisfactory.

Weekly instructions both for qualification in submarines and advancement in rating were given and all hands showed keen interest both in learning the boat and preparing themselves for the next higher rating.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS383) - Report of Fifth
War Patrol.

1. PAMPANITO's fifth war patrol was of 70 days duration, 10
of which were spent in the assigned area in the South China Sea. During
this period 5 night surface radar torpedo attacks were made firing a
total of 23 torpedoes.

2. Area coverage on this patrol was excellent; only part of
1 day was spent submerged.

3. The first three attacks were made on a convoy consisting
of one large AK or AP, one large AK or AO and one medium AK being escorted
by 4 escorts one of which was a CHIDORI type. The fourth and fifth attack
was made on a medium sized AK or AO which had one escort with her at time
attacks were made, the second escort being away from the formation.

(a) Attack No. 1: The first convoy was picked up in the late
afternoon by smoke being sighted in high periscope. Course
was set to gain position for night attack. PAMPANITO sub-
merged for about an hour after noting plane cover convoy at
low altitude. Position was gained ahead about four and half
hours after contact and an attack was made firing a total of
six torpedoes at the two nearest ships in formation. Two
hits were observed in the nearest and apparently largest ship
and ship went down by the stern. Radar pip decreased and
finally disappeared.

(b) Attack No. 2: After the first attack and subsequent evading
tactics which necessitated an end around run, an approach was
made on the two remaining ships which now had two of the
original four escorts with them. A total of six torpedoes
were again fired at these two ships and all missed due to
long range which allowed ships to maneuver and avoid.

Subject: U.S.S. PAMPANITO (SS383) - Report of Fifth War
Patrol - Comment on.

1. The Fifth War Patrol of the PAMPANITO under the command
of Commander P. E. SUMMERS, U.S.N., was of only twenty days total dur-
ation, but ten days in the SOUTH CHINA SEA were sufficient for her to
expend her torpedo load.

2. On 8 February, three night attacks were made on a convoy
consisting of three KAIHO and four A/S vessels. The first attack was
pressed home to the minimum possible range that excellent visibility
conditions permitted, and six torpedoes produced two hits which sank
a large AK. The PAMPANITO was able to elude the gun-firing escort. Two
more attacks were made that night, and every attempt to further exploit
the existing unfavorable submarine attack conditions was made, but ten
torpedoes produced no additional hits. The following night PAMPANITO
remained with BECUNA to execute a very clever stratagem. When
PAMPANITO was in position for attack, BECUNA fired a Very's Star. In
the ensuing confusion, which commenced when the starboard escort in-
vestigated, PAMPANITO scored two hits and blew up a medium AO. Again
a gun-firing escort was evaded on the surface.

3. The award of the Submarine Combat Insignie is authorized
for this patrol.

4. The Force Commander congratulates the Commanding Officer,
Officers and Crew of the PAMPANITO on a short, smart and aggressive
patrol during which the following damage was inflicted upon the enemy:

SUNK

1 - AK (Large - EU)7,500 Tons
1 - AO (Medium - EU)5,000 Tons
Total 12,500 Tons

(C) WEATHER

The northeast monsoon was steady in the mouth of the Gulf of Siam, south of Cochin China. Both wind and sea were from the northeast, with wind varying from about force two to force four. In general, the weather conditions followed closely those as described in coast pilot, with frequent overcast skies, some haziness, and light rain squalls.

From open to Saipan, encountered heavy weather almost daily, with heavy head seas. Skies were usually overcast.

(D) TIDAL INFORMATION

In the inner Gulf of Siam the set was to the southwest averaging about 0.9 knots. It was steady during March. Over near the Malay Coast off GREAT REDANG Island the set was southward about -0.5 knots. This corresponds with current as increased to about 1-2 knots along the coast, South of GREAT REDANG group the southerly current increased to about 1-2 knots along the coast.

(G) AIRCRAFT CONTACTS

We had 30 contacts with enemy planes while in the area and were bothered through-out the patrol by the efficient use of search planes. While no boat in our wolf pack was attacked at any instant that the Japs kept track of us and routed traffic where we were.

In all one instance all we have evidence of airborne radar, that on 23 March 1945. At no time on the area did we encounter planes at night.

By far the majority of our plane contacts were by radar so we have little information regarding types in operation.

On 21 March 1945 in position Lat. 05° 37' N. and Long. 104° 20' E., we sighted six wrecks of a Japanese plane in the water.

None.

(J) ANTI-SUBMARINE MEASURES AND EVASION TACTICS

Other than the SJ contact at extreme range on a possible high speed destroyer the night of 18 March 1945, the only contacts we had were with enemy planes. These occurred almost daily, both for us and for the other boats in the pack. Due to intermittent cloudy skies, very seldom were we able to have sight contact at prior to diving. At no time did any of these planes close us fast, nor did they attempt to drive home an attack on any of us although I am sure that we were sighted more than once. On one occasion while we were proceeding on surface at full speed during daylight to intercept a contact (as reported by one of the other submarines and which later was identified as a hospital ship) we were forced down three different times by enemy planes, which caused us to about 2 miles. Just prior to diving on one of these occasions, we sighted a Jap two-engine bomber escorted by a fighter circling us at 7-8 miles. At the time there were in all, five submarines including us running on the surface trying to intercept this ship contact and I am sure the Japs had us all under surveillance. In the meantime, it is possible that a convoy sneaked by us to the westward near the coast, because two days later a convoy was sighted west of Cape Krumus and south of Cape Jacques by one of our patrol planes in the vicinity. The intermittent cloudy skies and sometimes hazy weather make it expedient to use an intermittent sweep on SD radar during daylight hours (5 second sweep every 2-3 minutes) and it worked fine as far as detecting the aircraft, but in a positive test it was also a "Dead give-away" as to our location and that the Japs kept us pretty well spotted in both night and day by their detecting equipment.

(K) MAJOR DEFECTS AND DAMAGE

#2 and #4 Machinery - #2 air compressor motor flooded out when a plug in the main water circulating system carried away due to corrosion. Two shunt field coils and an interpole coil developed a zero ground and were replaced. #1 main engine has a cracked cylinder liner water jacket. This is the same defect which three liners were replaced during the last refit for this same defect. The crack occurred around the starting air adapter. When the starting air adapters to these cylinders were removed, it was found that they were badly pitted or corroded allowing exhaust gas to enter the water jacket probably causing the cracks.

#2 and #4 main motors again developed a badly unbalanced condition. This condition has occurred after running with 75% or more load for a period of

- 14 -
160:
Subject: U. S. S. POLLITO - Report of Sixth War Patrol.

24 hours or longer. The underexed occurs instantaneously with #2 trim motor taking the load. On previous occasions this has resulted in the brushes on #2 motor not are being burned. The first time this happened the load was taken off the motors before the brushes were burned and the brush rigging on #2 motor shifted until the load balanced. The motors have run satisfactorily since, with the brush rigging off the neutral point.

The gyro compass follow up motor failed due to overheating. The motor was removed and the spare installed. The bearing on the top of the vertical shaft of the follow up gear train was found to be scored causing the system to be very stiff. There is no spare bearing is carried it could not be replaced. The system was freed up as much as possible and the burned up motor is being repaired in the event it must be used again.

Ordnance and Gunnery - No major defects or damages occurred in the Ordnance and Gunnery equipment.

(L) RADIO

Two defects were experienced during this patrol. The "C" freq. band in the RBH receiver and H. F from 3.12 in one R.L Freq.

The signal from Bakers Fox faded daily between 0500 and 0700 zebra on all frequencies. A complete log of receiving conditions is being submitted to GNO as a separate report.

POLLITO cleared six messages to shore stations without too great delay; three direct to NPM and VIX6 and four via RBH. In all cases we received a receipt for them.

The best times to make were 2200, but the limits of the Wolf Pack Code were noted. POLLITO delivered one message to the U.L.M while she was anchored, but could not hear the JBF answer until she had surfaced. Each boat would have the best when diving for planes by sending a spare code group until the antenna went under. This was very successful at all times.

On 26 February 1945 we conducted several exercises with a Navy Search Plane with the idea of working out a procedure for smooth Lifo-submarine cooperation. A satisfactory system has now been worked out but we repeat here what we found in working with the plane for general information.

The biggest problem we always was the proper calibration of the two sets of equipment. When we first made rendezvous, the plane had been calling us by voice a half an hour without result, yet later we worked each other out to seventy miles and signal strength was never less than five.

Using VeryCall on the frequencies listed in Griffin able was not too satisfactory. 20 miles was about the maximum working range, but it is felt that this is not a fair indication as our voice modulation equipment is not the best and has given us trouble before.

JBF again proved unreliable at ranges over 15 miles. When the plane was overhead communications were good except when his bearing was 000° or 180° relative from us. On these bearings his signal and ours faded completely. A curious thing happened, when after diving and then surfacing, the plane noted that our signal strength on VHF for the same ranges was almost doubled. No explanation is offered for this.

Subject: U.S.S. POLLARDO - Report of Sixth War Patrol.

While submerged we successfully established communications with the plane using the SD mast. It is noted here that in a force three sea the plane lost our mast in a few minutes and could not pick it up again.

In making the rendezvous we picked the plane up at 16 miles by SD Radar and turned on our IFF. Until then the plane had no indication of our presence, but with the BN on, he homed on us readily and quickly rendezvoused with us. As a result of a conversation between Commander SEELEY and the Commanding Officer, the POLLARDO agreed to rendezvous each day with the plane covering our area to make a coordinated search and attack on any targets found. Because of a change in area assignments we did not have a chance to try our plan.

(c) RADAR

SJ-1 Radar - The SJ-1 operation was normal during this patrol. On 7 March 1945 two hours operational time were lost when the "A" Scope sweep disappeared. The trouble was a shorted C-33.1 in the power supply for the cathode ray tube. The intensity of the sweep in the range indicator was increasing gradually. On 19 March 1945 a thorough check was made of the circuit but the trouble could not be found. To restore the intensity control potentiometer, P-11 (25,000 ohms.) was replaced by a spare P-8 (70,000 ohms.). The low side of P-8 (70,000 ohms.) was connected to the center tap to reduce the voltage drop across one potentiometer. Reliable ranges were as follows:

SD-4 Radar - The SD-4 performance was excellent during the entire patrol. No operational difficulties were encountered. All aircraft were detected at a range of eight miles or greater.

SJ-1 & SD-1 - On 5 March 1945, the power transformer in the SJ-1 unit developed a short after approximately 500 hours of operation. This is the second transformer that has failed after this period of operation. Operation was restored when the transformer was replaced by a spare one on board.

BN - The power transformer of the BN shorted on 25 March 1945. As no spare was carried for this transformer, the BN was inoperative for the remainder of the patrol.

(d) SOUND GEAR AND SOUND CONDITIONS

Because the time submerged this patrol was short, no comment can be made on sound conditions.

The charging condensers in the JP-1 receiver developed a low resistance to ground but this did not effect the operation of the equipment. The training shaft was noisy in rotation and reduced the efficiency of the operator.

(B) DENSITY LAYERS

Bathythermograph Cards were taken for each dive made on station. The shallow water in the assigned patrol area limited the deepest dive to 150 feet.

In both calm seas and zone of force five the cards with but one exception were is-thermal, the one exception being for the dive of 7 March 1945 in 37 fathoms of water and with seas and wind of force one. This card showed an is-ballast to 60 feet, a negative gradient of 1.0 from 60 feet to 80 feet and an is-ballast from 80 feet to 120 feet.

The temperature of the surface water varied from 80° to 82° F., while the temperature of the air varied from 77° to 84°.

(F) HEALTH, FOOD AND HABITABILITY

The health in general was good. There were several colds the first week after leaving Subic Bay. One arm was on the binnacle list for two weeks with a fever from cold.

The meals were well planned and served, except that 354 lbs. of meat spoiled and had to be surveyed thereby limiting the menu slightly.

Being the first boat to refit in Subic Bay, the recreational facilities there were very limited. The crew lived on board during the refit.

(G) PERSONNEL

The conduct of the personnel on board during this run was very satisfactory and in keeping with the highest traditions of the Naval Service.

(9) REMARKS

Since the PIPERITO had spent her last patrol in this area (S-2) and had made its only two contacts on enemy convoys well to seaward of the mouth of the Gulf of Siam, and not knowing that some of the northbound traffic moved well inside the Gulf we considered it both wise and feasible for the pack to remain at sea and to put patrol line in this area to cover the most likely routes for shipping both inshore and to seaward. In order to do this thoroughly, and to co-ordinate during daylight was almost a necessity. This method has been described in the narrative of patrol with no contacts.

The PIPERITO having had only a short run from Subic to the area had ample fuel to continue her patrolling during daylight the remainder of the patrol, which has either sentries not so well-supplied, having come up from Australia, and in order to conserve our southern boundary of area so extended from 6° 00' N to 5° 00' N in order to give us a shorter and more compact area- not patrol line from the Malay Coast eastward and allow port time submerged patrolling for the other boats. This request was granted and at the same time Command was ordered to join our pack.

At this time an east-west staggered patrol line was established between Lats. 5° and 6° N. from the Malay Coast eastward for about 150 miles. The two boats inshore on this line remained submerged during daylight to avoid detection or sinkings while the two boats to seaward maintained surface cruising. It was while using this plan that the SEALION sank an unescorted tanker off the coast at night, and we were the only contact to seaward with a high speed destroyer, although we were unable to close for an attack. There were two pilots contacts made by the pack prior to our leaving the patrol area, at which time the Commanding Officer of the SEALION became ComSubPac. This will in turn be covered, the PIPERITO remained on the surface at all times, except when diving for plane contacts and for one day while effecting repairs to gyro compass, in order to maintain radio guard and to coordinate disposition of wolfpack in case of contacts.

Subject: U.S.S. BATFISH - Report of Sixth War Patrol; Comments on.

1. The Sixth War Patrol of the U.S.S. BATFISH was conducted in the Gulf of Siam during the period 25 February - 24 April 1945. Two 17-seawar days were spent in the area, one day submerged. The Commanding Officer was also in command of a group consisting of Batfish, Caiman, Guilla and Piper.

2. This patrol was characterized by almost complete lack of targets. Only one possibly suitable target was encountered. She was making 22 knots and the Terponite was unable to attain a firing position. She was not seen; her have been a destroyer. Thirty plane contacts were made but the submarine not attacked. No plane contacts were made at night. There was only one indication of airborne radar. Eight floating mines were sighted.

3. The SD radar was used by keying about 5 seconds every 2 to 3 minutes. The C.O. states that the SD was fine for detecting planes but undoubtedly kept the Japs advised of the Submarine's approximate location. The evidence is rather conclusive that this is precisely what happens when either the SD or SJ is used very much. They are detected and DF'd. Though the Japs cannot actually home, traffic will not be routed through that area and search planes will cover the submarine. The instantaneous keyed SD with persistent scope partially solves the SD problem. Possibly the Japs cannot even detect ST yet and its use as a search radar might be indicated. It does not, however, have the range of the SJ. When SD or SJ are used for search purposes the keying must be at irregular intervals, as done by the Terponite.

Subject: British and Australian Prisoner-of-War Survivors - Rescue of.

(A) NARRATIVE

On the afternoon of 15 September 1944, while patrolling on the surface on an easterly heading from HAINAN ISLAND in the South China Sea, at Latitude 18° 42' N., Longitude 114° 00' E., the O.O.D. and bridge lookouts sighted a lifeboat and a large quantity of debris floating on the surface of a calm sea. This spot was a little to the north of where an enemy convoy had been intercepted and attacked by our submarines on the night of 11-12 September 1944. There was a possibility of the lifeboat being occupied so course was altered to go alongside, only to find it abandoned. At this time, 1610(I), a lookout reported that there were two rafts on the horizon with men on them. It was naturally believed that these would be Japanese, so small arms were broken out and preparations made for taking prisoners.

On the approach to the first raft, which was a makeshift affair of hatch covers and timbers, it was noted that the fifteen men it contained were thickly covered with crude-oil and were clothed very scantily, though some had nondescript hats and a few wore the regulation Japanese soldier's caps. They were waving frantically and all shouting at will so that no words could be distinguished, although one voice was finally heard to speak distinctly in English. While getting the raft alongside, orders were given to bring aboard the English speaking man, and by the time the first line was over the amazing announcement came to the bridge, "They are British and Australian Prisoner-of-War and Japs survivors.

All hands went into action immediately; those below decks sent up bales of rags and began preparing hot soup and tea in quantities; the pharmacist's mate assembled his gear for immediate treatment, and the rescue party commenced bringing the survivors aboard. The poor fellows were so frantic with joy at this unbelievable piece of good fortune that they began jumping from the raft and trying to clamber up the sides of the ship. Members of the rescue party dived over the side to make the raft fast, herded the survivors back onto the raft and aided them up to the ship's deck. The weakened condition of these men, as well as their covering of slippery crude-oil, made the actual recovery quite difficult. Some of them could help themselves, but the majority had to be lifted and dragged aboard bodily.

The next problem was to clean some of the oil from their bodies and to treat their immediate needs before sending them below. While this job was being done the second raft was reached and the true bearings taken of three others within sight. The second raft contained nine men who fortunately were comparatively free from oil, making the problem of bringing them aboard much easier. While heading for the next group, a small raft was passed close aboard with its single occupant dead with part of the head gone (Probably by a shark). Recovered third and fourth raft-loads of eleven emaciated ex-prisoners-of-war. Another small raft was sighted with one figure lying motionless on his back. He seemed to be still alive and when one of the ship's crew dived into the water with a line, he sat up, startled and started to go over the side. The man in the water persuaded him to remain seated until he could be helped aboard. This man was almost blind and in a semi-conscious condition when brought aboard and remained unconscious almost continuously until he died the following evening.

(A) NARRATIVE (Continued)

While the eleven men from the next raft were being brought aboard the after lookout reported "Three planes in formation astern". There were approximately fifty men topside at this time including bridge personnel and the rescue squad as well as many survivors who had as yet not been lowered down the hatch. Fortunately one of the planes was seen to flap its wings proving the formation to be large birds gliding in perfect order.

This completed the rescue of all survivors in the immediate vicinity, but a bearing had been taken on a raft now out of sight to the south, so the ship was headed in that direction at high speed. At 1810, two rafts were sighted ahead and soon thirteen more survivors were being rescued. While getting the men from the last of these two rafts the high periscope watch sighted another raft at 020° T. and also what appeared to be a ship's masts bearing 037° T. at the extreme range of vision. While unable to verify this report of the raft, the ship was identified as a submarine that appeared to have a gun aft, making us very suspicious, since one of the survivors had stated that a German submarine was somewhere in this area (later proved to be SEALION with men on deck aft) and since it did not look or signal like an American, we dived to periscope depth and after identifying and watching the submarine for a few minutes through the periscope and noting that it was practically dead in the water, decided that it must be the SEALION rescuing survivors. We since we had sent a message to her earlier requesting that she come over and assist in rescue. So surfaced and resumed searching. It was almost completely dark by this time. A single man on a small raft was seen waving what appeared to be a white flag, but he was at some time, but later proved to be his "bleached hand". He was recovered and course was set for the last raft that had been sighted before diving. This raft was luckily located in the dark and another twelve men were rescued and stowed below making a total of seven-three (73) survivors on board.

Once below decks the main problem was the examination to determine the injuries and sicknesses. In this respect, DEEDS, M.L., PhM1c, USN, showed tireless energy and outstanding professional knowledge of the highest order. The survivors most acute need was water, which they were given in small quantities through the rags followed by hot tea, soup or broth for those who were conscious. As all these men were suffering from acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, starvation, dehydration and skin sores, their needs were many, but since the ship had necessarily to retain its military efficiency, and since it was not known what contagious diseases some of them might have, it was decided to place all but six of the most critical cases in the after torpedo room (the six were put on bunks in one corner of the after battery compartment) where, even though it was more difficult to tend their needs, they could be isolated until given a more thorough examination. One head was set aside for the use of the survivors; they were given separate eating utensils which were washed and stowed apart from those of the crew, and two officers and several crew members were assigned the nursing detail. The entire crew showed an exemplary attitude and volunteered cheerfully to do all tasks and make any sacrifices that would help the survivors in any way.

(B) TREATMENT OF SURVIVORS WHILE ON BOARD

The general condition of the survivors when rescued was critical, with every man suffering from acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, starvation, dehydration and salt sores. About seventy percent of these men had drunk sea water, urine or blood during their four days on the rafts, and nearly all were covered with fuel oil.

As the survivors were brought aboard they were treated on deck as follows: the crude-oil was wiped and then sponged off with diesel oil, and morphine was administered to those suffering from extreme shock (15 syrettes being used in this time). As soon as emergency cleaning and shock treatment were given, the men were lowered through the after battery hatch, given a cup of hot tea, a sip of not vegetable soup, after which each was given an eye irrigation followed by Butyn Sulfate and Boric Acid Ointment was applied to ease the irritation on the skin of each man's scrotum. This irritation being caused by the crude-oil.

Six of the more critical cases, who were given bunks in the after battery compartment, had their sores and ulcerations cleaned with Azochloramide in Triscetin 1:500 and dressed with Sulfathiazole Ointment 5%.

About one quarter of the survivors were given sedatives of Phenobarbital or Sodium Amytal, depending upon each one's condition. Three men had rather severe cases of malaria, one of whom was in a state of delirium for four hours after being rescued. These men were given Quinine Hydrochloride grs. XX followed by grs. X every four hours. Two men found to have severe Cellutitis infections were placed in bunks with parts elevated and dosed with Sulfadiazine grs. XV with Sodium Bicarbonate at four hour intervals rather than the prescribed dose of 4 gm. of Sulfa, because of their condition. One man was found to have an injured back and a broken rib, but due to the acute tropical dermatitis infection which covered fifty percent of his body no strapping was done. This dermatitis infection was treated with Sulfathiazole Ointment covered with cotton dressing to make the man more comfortable in his bunk.

By twelve hours after the rescue every man had received an examination and had had his worse sores cleaned with Azochloramide in Triscetin 1:500 and dressed with Sulfa-thiazole Ointment 5% or Sulfadiazine powder depending on each individual's condition. Upon questioning the men, it was found that during their two and a half years of imprisonment all had had some degree of malaria; seventy percent had suffered from Pellagra or Beri Beri; fifty percent were affected by tropical dermatitis infections and all but three or four had Gingivitis or Vicents Angina. It was also learned that all had been exposed to Cholera, Dysentery, Typhus Fever, and other types of contagious diseases, so that although, during their time on board, no one showed any signs of having contracted any of these diseases, precautions were taken to keep isolated all cups, utensils, the head, etc. Within three hours after examination each survivor was receiving one cup of either water, tea with sugar and milk, cocoa or soup every hour for twenty-four hours.

The only casualty occurred the day following the rescue. This man died of acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, dehydration and possible internal hemorrhage. He had been in a state of delirium almost continuously since being brought aboard. 1. Story of ANDERSON, C., #59AMO38, Lance Corporal, 5th Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire Regiment, British Army - On January 29, 1942, the U.S.S. WEST POINT sailed into Singapore Harbor under the eyes of the Japanese bombers and unloaded her cargo of the ill-fated 18th Infantry Division, British Army.

We were taken to transit camps in our own battalion in readiness to go up to the front lines to fight that savage and inhuman enemy the devil's of the East (Japs). My battalion went up to the front lines on the 12th of Feb. and it was then we knew what hell was. Fifth column was dead against us and we had no air support at all. Friday, the 13th of February, 1942, was a day never to be forgotten by any of us. Bombs rained on us from everywhere, and men were being slaughtered left and right. Sunday, the 15th of February 1942, at 1600 a BR came along and gave order of unconditional surrender.

We were now P.O.Ws. of the Japs. Hunger had taken us and it was a very downhearted army that marched 16 miles to the Changi Barracks on the 17th.

From then on, up to October 14, 1944, we were worked on buildings and salvage dumps, and the guards over us were like slave drivers with a whip in their hand. Our pay per day, by the time we had finished a day's work we had earned $25.00. Our food consisted of broken rice and a very small ration of fish and seaweed. On 14th May, we were taken to Thailand to build a railroad from Bankok,to Moeean in Burma. We travelled through Malaya in railway trucks with 32 men in each. We marched 150 miles through Thailand, through uninhabited jungles and rice fields - up to our knees in mud and slime. The only mean beings we saw were the wild hillmen of Siam, in their own kampongs with a score or so of water buffalo wallowing in the mud. Men were falling in their tracks and the guards were beating them with split lengths of bamboo. We arrived at our first jungle home on 21st and we had to sleep in mosquito-infested swamps. This place was called Wampo and it was here we found what living hell was. We lost 27 men within a month and things were coming very hard for us. Food consisted of plain rice and salt water for well over the first month. Men were being ill-treated by the Japs in every shape and form, working from dawn to dusk clearing virgin jungle and rock for this thought-impossible, mad idea. Men of other jungle working battalions were marching through our camp every day to settle in other jungle camps, made of bamboo and atop huts, further up the river. The British Officer in charge of our camp was a man who will never be forgotten by those who knew him. He was known as the "Grand Old Man of the River", Colonel Lilley of the 1/5 Forresters, and it was through his stubborness that the Japs made things slightly easier for us. Disease was hitting all camps by now, and the river which was called Leie Laie, was soon known as the "River of Death". The first Christmas arrived and the Japs opened their hearts and gave us two old cows for 1500 men.

In January, 1943, the word came through that the railroad had to be finished within one year, and so the work must be speeded up. As the work sped up, so did the death rate, and the beatings-up by these small savages. We had a little extra food, consisting of fresh vegetables and buffalo meat, but the things we wanted were medical supplies which were absolutely refused. As one Jap officer said, "If a man is ill, let him die! The work must go on. This was Lt. Lannice, whom I hope has met a worse death than any man taken prisoner.

A. Story of BARNES, H.D., #271190, Private, 4th Royal Norfolk Regiment, British Army - On 29 October 1941, the 18th Division left Liverpool, England for convoy to the East. I was one of the guys in an infantry battalion in the 54th Brigade, 18th Division, British Army.

We left on a foggy morning. Sorry to see the coast fade away in the distance; it was au revoir to dear old England. Soon were riding over the waves of the Atlantic Ocean. On November 9th we arrived in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Transferred to U.S.S.WAKEFIELD, U.S.M.T. MOUNT VERNON, LEONARD WOOD, and another smaller transport. Left for Trinidad, West Indies on November 11, 1941. Arrived there escorted by American cruisers and destroyers, also aircraft carrier, LEXINGTON. Left for Capetown, South Africa on November 14, 1941. Arrived December 8, 1941. Had good shore leave - 4 days. Left Capetown for India on December 12, 1941. Arrived December 29, 1941. Left Bombay, India, January 18th, 1942 for Singapore. Arrived Singapore January 27, 1942. Japanese troops had already taken most of Malaya, we were put in first line of defense on February 9, 1942.

There was nothing much to do until the Nip troops landed on Singapore the night of February 9, 1942. We were all ready for them. All through the night heavy guns pounded the coast, more fell in our yards short of our positions. At dawn, they halted. It was reported thousands of Japanese troops had been killed, but they had landed enough coast on the west side to get their mortars into action against our defense lines. We were under mortar fire for a two-hour, continuous barrage. Ahead of our lines, green gun carriers were maneuvering for positions to attack these mortars; but had to return owing to direct machine-gunning and bombing of the roads and areas around.

My platoon (mortar) was ordered into action at 7 o'clock. The first barrage silenced a nest of Jap mortars almost at once, so we waited for awhile. Suddenly our section patrols appeared with several men short, telling us a battalion of Japs were only a few hundred yards from our positions. We had orders to pick up and withdraw, but our section commander asked for one mortar to stay in position. We volunteered. I was given a tommy gun with six others, one each, who ordered to go to forward positions to cover mortar if they had to withdraw. Suddenly there was a crash behind us; we threw ourselves down. Looking back to where it came from we saw there was nothing left of the mortar or the two operators. They were the first casualties we had; but not the last, for out of the sky they came, mortar shell upon mortar shell, crashing and smashing down upon the platoon withdrawing. Every mortar of the platoon was smashed, parts lying all around along the road side; and our mortar shells were exploding; deadly shrapnel flying amongst us. 18 were killed and 10 wounded. It was a hopeless scene. Me and the section commander were the only six left, owing to the fact we were down flat.

We waited there until the Jap mortars halted their firing, then ran for the deep drains by the roadside. The Japs must have used at least 20 mortars. On the way up to our lines, was the start of the hell on earth. We had nothing but tommy guns left, only 4 of them between us; but we had to stay in our positions with not a hope of getting a chance to get the Jap mortars and save the rifle companys from the deadly murder in their lines.

Nothing could hold them back. Everywhere we turned, men were falling, killed or wounded by bits of awful barrage from all around.

As suddenly as it started, it ceased. All was deadly silence. Our ears were ringing, and our eyes were smarting from the gas of the explosions. Fellows could be heard groaning and shouting way back for help. The stretcher bearers were running back and forth. When I came to my senses properly, carrying back smashed bodies that were still alive but never could be made whole again.

Signals could be seen fixing the field wireless, trying to get communications with the rifle company; officers were giving orders to them, but not a sound could they get from their sets to assure us of any help, for we got the orders by signal from them to run for it to our right into the rubber forests. I don't remember much of that mad dash for what we thought would be cover.

I came to my senses in a dugout in a quarry, a continuous crashing of mortars was going on all around. I could see the earth flying towards the centre of where the rifle companys were in position, or they were originally supposed to be. Suddenly I saw a group of figures running, bent double almost, toward our dugout. We could see that they were riflemen battalion runners. Two only got through, the other three were smashed to pieces by a mortar that crashed above them on an overhanging rock. The two fell through the top of our dugout, at our feet, O.K., but shaken. They told us we were surrounded by Japs. Out off from the rest, we stayed in the dugout for three days not daring to move for each time bullets would smash the rock above our heads if we did.

The night of February 12th, 1942, we made for the road again, knowing we were inside enemy lines, dreaming each moment that out of the darkness would come the rattle of machine guns and maybe death for some of us. We got safely to the trenches by the roadside and three ourselves in, waited, then crawled like cats on our bellies for mile upon mile, keeping over obstacles in our way. It was only God's mercy that I wasn't hit by it; these red hot jagged bits of steel.

We waited not daring to move. It came into sight, a Bren Gun Carrier, with its body torn and holed by shrapnel. It was one of our own, by the division sign on its gun covers. As its body came alongside misfiring and knocking, we saw one of our boys was driving it. Recognized his tortured looking face. We all clamored up the bank and gave him a yell to stop. He pulled up, thank God, we climbed on and away we tore down the road, praying, I was, that we could get back to our H.Q. which was the other side of Sukit Timah Race Course. How we got there was a miracle. We were fired upon by guns at the road barrier held by the Japs. We saw them throwing themselves down behind their machine guns. They must have been poor shots for not one hit us as we roared past them, looking through slots in the side of the moving truck. What a chance it was. We yelled as the Bren Gunner on my right side fired. We saw the first two Japs throw up their arms and fall, as his bullets hit them. They vanished from sight of us, as we turned a bend. We got through to H.Q. and found our boys had lost lots of mates getting back to safety from those deadly mortars, out of range and sight.

We were given food and tea, then our Section Commander told us all how grave the situation was on all the lines. Mortars had killed and wounded hundreds, it was impossible to hold a front line without reenforcements and there was no reinforcements, as hundreds were surrounded by Japs. We waited in dugouts for further orders from Division H.Q. It was a lot different to anything we expected, although things were critical.

The orders were to lay down our arms.

I remember only too well the first thought that came to my head, it was all over, I was safe, alive. We must all have thought very much the same thing. None of us could speak, it couldn't be true, but true it was. I'll never forget the look upon our Colonel's face, when he told us we were beaten. Tears were running down his face and he turned away, waving us to the positions we were to go in order to give ourselves over to the little yellow bastards, that were to be seen ahead of us with their guns aiming at us.

They waited until we were all lined up. Then each man was searched by a Jap soldier. They took our watches, rings and anything of any value and then the officers (Japanese) gave us orders to the effect that we would be treated as prisoner-of-war and told us to obey all orders, or we would be shot. They also told us that the conditions of surrender were still in the early stages. However, General Percival, and all the G.H.Q. of the British and Australian Forces were in conference at the Ford Motor Works Factory at Bukit Timah, and if conditions were agreed to by the Japanese we would be treated well. All their orders were agreed to by Governor General Percival and the results were that we were Japanese Prisoners-of-War. Later we learned that slaves would have been a much more appropriate word to have used.
