206:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

NARRATIVE

28 October 1944

1530 (H) USS DARTER, PIPEFISH and SEACAT underway from Pearl Harbor, T.H. to Midway in accordance with ComTaskForce Seventeen Operation Order No. 302-44. Conducted independent training and exercised at communication drills enroute.

1 November 1944

0900 (H) Arrived Midway. Fueled to capacity. All boats effected minor repairs. U.S.S. SEACAT delayed in departing until 2 November 1944 due to extensive repairs to "Sail Dog" radar. U.S.S. SEAHAVEN joined the pack. Orders for pack changed by Comsubpac despatch 061022 of November, 1944, directing us to proceed to Saipan for fuel and thence to patrol Convoy College. Assigned area destroy west of Longitude 116° E.
1530 (H) U.S.S. TILEFISH, PIPEFISH and SEAHAVEN underway for Saipan. Exercised at communications and held independent training enroute.

5 November 1944

1100 (H) U.S.S. PIPEFISH reported a case of acute appendicitis on board; left group and proceeded to Saipan at maximum sustained speed.

7 November 1944

0637 (H) U.S.S. ARCHERFISH joined up for remainder of trip to Saipan.

9 November 1944

1330 (H) U.S.S. DARTER and SEAHAVEN arrived Saipan. Commanding Officer, U.S.S. PIPEFISH reported cracked liners on No. 4 main engine, estimated repairs would be effected by 1100, 11 November 1944. Boats fueled to capacity and effected minor repairs.

- 1 -
207:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

10 November 1944

1100 (H) U.S.S. BIGHT arrived Saipan, fueled to capacity and effected minor voyage repairs.

11 November 1944

1345 (H) U.S.S. PINTADO, SEACAT, PIPEFISH and SEARAVEN underway for patrol area at two engine speed.

15 November 1944

0638 (H) Increased speed to standard speed on four main engines to intercept a reported convoy. Assigned other boats to stations across track of expected convoy.

16 November 1944

Patrolled submerged on assigned station.

1720 (H) No contact developed, so set course for run at two engine speed.

17 November 1944

0000 (H) Entered assigned patrol area at 19° 20' N., 116° E. Conducting surface patrol on course 240° T., using high periscope watch. This method of patrol was employed enroute to and in the area.
2100 (H) Commenced patrol on course 220° - 040° T. at one engine speed in a lane which roughly parallels the eastern coast of HAINAN. Other boats in pack are to patrol in parallel lanes on arrival tonight or tomorrow. SEARAVEN to westward along the area boundary, PIPEFISH and SEACAT to eastward of PINTADO.

18 November 1944

1940 (H) U.S.S. PIPEFISH reported a radar contact at Lat. 19° 32' N., Long. 111° 50' E. Ordered all boats to proceed to intercept and attack.
2047 (H) U.S.S. PINTADO had SJ contact, 10,000 yards and proceeded to

- 2 -

3
208:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

track convoy. Radar indicates three ships, two large ones and an escort. PIPEFISH reported she was attacking. Enemy course 220° T., speed 10 knots. SEARAVEN closed and took position 6000 yards on port beam of PAMPANITO.

2330 (H)Received report from PIPEFISH that she had broken off attack due to SJ radar interference on bearing of target and suspected it to be a submarine. No boat was challenged however.
2332 (H)Sent out message PAMPANITO attacking and headed in.
2323 (H)At a range of 2700 yards, using a 1° divergent spread, gyro angle about 340°, and on 60 port track, commenced firing bow tubes on radar bearings. Fired six torpedoes at the leading ship which was the largest. Since it was very rough,spread torpedoes in depth 2 ft. - 6 ft. alternately. Position Lat. 19°08'N., Long.111°28'E.
2324 (H)Completed firing bow tubes, swung right with full rudder.
2326 (H)Commenced firing stern tubes on 100 port track on second target. Range 2700 yards.
2326-30 (H)Heard and saw two hits in the first target. One at MOT and the second near the stern. A bright orange flame accompanied the hits, followed immediately by an enormous pillar of black smoke about 500 ft. high. The fire subsided and went out in almost two minutes at which time target disappeared from sight and radar screen.
2326-10 (H)Completed firing the stern tubes at the second ship.
2327 (H)Heard and felt one more hit and saw flash on bearing of second target. As second ship did not disappear from radar screen ordered SEARAVEN to attack. PAMPANITO trailed and made reload. Target group changed course to 300° T. and headed for the coast of HAINAN

- 3 -
209:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

at speed of about 10 knots, group now consisting of one freighter and escort.

0605 (H) SEARAVEN reported she had completed two attacks but had made no hits. Believe misses were due to high seas and shallow depth settings used by SEARAVEN. At this point no boat was in position to make an attack before the target could reach the beach south of TOROEN POINT on HAINAN, so ordered boats to return to patrol stations previously assigned. It was extremely rough and dark, making identification difficult, but it is believed that the results of the attack were: Sunk by PAMPANITO: one large freighter about 6,000 tons. Damaged by PAMPANITO: one freighter about 5,000 tons.
0731 (H) Felt two heavy explosions but no one else in the pack claimed making any attacks. Possibly the cripple had more difficulty.

20 November to 28 November 1944

Pack continued to patrol in lanes parallel to HAINAN coast with PAMPANITO patrolling along western boundary of Area and the other boats in lanes parallel twenty-five miles apart respectively to the eastward. During this period the only contacts were with patrol planes; from three to four daily and an occasional plane contact during the nights of bright moonlight. Six patrol boats, trawler type were contacted on several occasions near the northwest corner of the area. These furnished no strain however.

29 November 1944

2102 (H) PAMPANITO had SJ contact bearing 094° T., range 24,000 yards. Just started to track and develop this when, at 2110, SD contact.

- 4 -

5
210:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

4 miles. Dived. (A clear night, flat calm, and full moon).

2130 (H)Surfaced. Sent out contact report to other ships.
2200 (H)Regained radar contact at 25,000 yards.
2210 (H)SD contact 8 miles, which closed to 5 miles. Dived.
2238 (H)Surfaced.
2252 (H)Regained SJ contact and commenced five hour end around in bright moonlight. None of the other boats were in a position to get in an attack at this time.

30 November 1944

0419 (H)Dived for dawn submerged attack.
0500-30 (H)PAMPANITO fired six torpedoes from bow tubes. Three each at the two leading ships, identified as tankers, on track angles of 110° P. Range 4000 yards, Speed 16 knots, with a 2° divergent spread, depth setting 4 feet. Five torpedo explosions were heard about 8 minutes after firing. These must have been end of run explosions as no evidence of hits was seen. This was an exceptionally large percentage of end of run explosions however, as none were experienced with the first ten torpedoes fired by this submarine. Position of attack Lat, 17° 47' N, Long. 110° 30' E. PAMPANITO was forced deep and on surfacing an hour and a half later was unable to relocate the convoy before being forced down by planes. A search of the vicinity of this attack rendered no evidence of hits.

PAMPANITO returned to patrol station.

30 November to 3 December 1944

Patrolling area. No contacts except with planes. Weather turned bad and by 2 December 1944 we were in the throes of a northeast monsoon with high seas and continuous rain.

- 5 -
211:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

2 December 1944

0040 (H) SEARAVEN reported radar contact from estimated position Lat. 19° 30' N., Long. 119° 14' E. Ordered all boats to close and attack. SEARAVEN's reported convoy consisted of 4 large AO's, 1 AP, 1 AK, and 1 unidentified ship plus 4 escorts, base course 220° T., speed 12 to 13 knots.
0410 (H) SEARAVEN reported completion of 1st attack, position 18° 40' N., 111° 57' E., and reported one AP sunk with two hits.
0440 (H) SEACAT reported completion of attack with one AO sunk with two hits from 700 yards range, position Lat. 18° 42' N., Long. 111° 55' E.
0547 (H) SEARAVEN completed second attack and reported sinking a large AO and damaging another, position Lat. 18° 40' N., Long. 111° 52' E. PAROANITO saw flash as SEARAVEN's first AO blew up.
0544 (H) PIPEFISH reported attack completed with one timed hit in an AK, position Lat. 18° 35' N., Long. 111° 45' E. PIPEFISH reported that there were four ships altogether in convoy plus two escorts when she made her attack. An hour later when PAROANITO made an attack there were only three ships left so believe PIPEFISH sank the AK. At any rate in the PAROANITO attack there were two AO's plus one unidentified ship.
0655 (H) PAROANITO made submerged attack and fired four torpedoes at the leading AO, position Lat. 18° 25' N., Long. 111° 35' E. Both AO's were close together but not quite over-lapping. PAROANITO had much difficulty to keep from broaching as the waves were 30 feet high. Four torpedo explosions were heard one of which is

- 6 -
212:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

believed to have been a hit. The target group zigged away prior to firing and a firing range of 3200 yards was estimated. Escorts forced PAMPANITO down so that results were not observed and by the time the ensuing depth charging was over, target group was out of sight. The PAMPANITO used eight foot depth settings.

Three of these torpedo explosions were within 10 seconds of each other at the end of the run. The first explosion was 6 minutes after firing with the other three 8 minutes after firing. Again the Commanding Officer of the PAMPANITO points out the high percentage of end of run explosions. This now made eight out of ten end of run explosions out of the last ten torpedoes, while none were experienced with the first ten torpedoes.

Contact with the enemy was not regained. The SEARAVEN and the SEACAT remained in contact with the SEARAVEN's cripple which had two escorts. The SEACAT reported one ship with two escorts, speed 12 knots which was believed at first to be the remains of the convoy, this ship later slowed to 4 knots and turned out to be the damaged AO from the SEARAVEN's second attack. The SEACAT sank this cripple during the night, position Lat. 17° 45' N, Long. 111° 20' E. Results from this combined attack appear to be; for the SEARAVEN, sunk 1 AP and 1 AO and damaged another AO. For the SEACAT; sunk 2 AO's. For the PIPEFISH; sunk 1 AK. For the PAMPANITO, damaged 1 AO.

4 December to 16 December 1944

Continued to patrol in lance off HAINAN coast. Weather continued
213:
GROUP COMMANDER'S REPORT OF WAR PATROL

foul, seas high with wind from the northeast. On 5 December 1944 ordered SEARAVEN who was out of torpedoes to return to base. No contacts were developed but numerous mines, life rafts, trees and debris was sighted at various times. Much ammunition was expended trying to explode floating mines but because of high seas no success was had. Pack was granted one week extension in area by Comsubpac. No contacts other than with planes were made during this entire period.

17 December 1944

0455 (H) PIPEFISH reported radar contact Lat. 18° 40' N., Long. 111° 12' E. This developed into a single large freighter making 11 knots along the southeast coast of HAINAN. The PIPEFISH made an unsuccessful attack about 0600 but was unable to make an end around before the target entered SAILOW BAY. Neither the SEACAT nor RAZANITO were able to get into the picture.

18 December 1944

Because of low fuel the RAZANITO departed the area for Fremantle in accordance with Comsubpac's serial 180121 of December, 1944 after turning over command of the Pack to Commander R. R. McGREGOR, U.S. Navy, Commanding Officer of the U.S.S. SEACAT. The Groupe Commander wishes to express at this time, his appreciation to the Commanding Officers of the SEACAT, PIPEFISH, and SEARAVEN for their wholehearted cooperation and for the agressive manner in which they conducted this arduous patrol. At this point it is believed that the following damage was inflicted on the enemy during this patrol:

U.S.S. SEARAVEN (SS196) - Report of.

1. Forwarded, readdressed via The Commander Submarines SEVENTH FLEET
and The Commander SEVENTH FLEET.

2. This attack group under the command of Captain P.E. PIHL(N), Jr.
conducted in the area adjacent to the east coast of Saigon. The group entered
the area on 17 November and operated most effectively in developing contacts and
making attacks. SEARAVEN was returned to base on 5 December after
experiencing torpedoes. PIPEFISH departed from the group on 10 December
final routine obtained by the SEACAT and PIPEFISH are not yet known.

3. On 12 November a contact was developed by PIPEFISH which enabled
SEARAVEN to attack an escorted convoy and to destroy one AK while damaging another AK. SEARAVEN then made two attacks but obtained no hits. Again on 20
November PIPEFISH was able to complete an end around on a convoy and make an
attack on the two leading ships which were identified as AO. No hits were in
evidence. On 3 December SEARAVEN contacted a seven ship convoy with four escorts
and delivered two attacks to dispose of 1 AP, 1 AO and to damage another AO. In
the meantime SEACAT attacked from very short range to obtain two hits for the
sinking of 1 AO. Shortly thereafter PIPEFISH delivered her attack and probably
sank 1 AK. This event was quickly followed by a SEARAVEN attack at two overlapping AO's which damaged one of the AO's. In a night attack SEACAT regained
attack position and polished off the AO previously damaged by SEARAVEN.

The only other contact and attack was made by PIPEFISH on 17
December which resulted in no hits.

4. The Squadron Commander heartily congratulates the Group Commander
and the three commanding officers with him upon the close working unit which they
developed to produce very severe damage upon enemy shipping. Their fine courage,
aggressiveness and teamwork is inspirational.

C. C. BURLINGAME
Acting.

REPORT OF COORDINATED ATTACK GROUP 17.14

(A) PROLOGUE.

ComSubPac Operation Order #43-45 of 10 February 1945 formed a coordinated attack group to be known as BENNETT'S BLAZERS, consisting of the SEA OWL (SS405), PIRANHA (SS389) and PUFFER (SS268) with task unit designations 17.14.1, 17.14.2, and 17.14.3 respectively. Commanding Officer SEA OWL was designated O.T.C. 17.14. All units of the group were refitting at GUAM with ECS session in the new Convoy College at Camp Dealey, followed by a conference of C.O.'s and communications personnel in which it was determined that all of the group saw eye-to-eye on the principles of group operations. Since the operation order directed the group to proceed to CONVOY COLLEGE and "conduct offensive patrol in accordance with dispatch instructions to be furnished" the usual detailed advance planning was not considered feasible.

(B) NARRATIVE

11 February

1500 IUnderway from APRA HARBOR, GUAM, rendezvoused with DRUM (SS228) and escort U.S.S. ROB (DM18) at channel entrance, and set course for local operating area S-3.
1720 ISEA OWL left formation to conduct gun practice on target towed by GREENPLET while remainder of group patrolled to Northward. This delay proved ill-advised as it lead to our becoming involved with a surface task force and entering safety lane well behind our schedule. It would have been preferable to have had the ship involved proceed ahead to conduct practice and then join up with group on schedule.
2153Entered safety lane some three hours behind submarine notice. Escort turned back and DRUM pulled ahead to maintain 15 knots speed of advance. PIRANHA was assigned lane 12 miles to starboard and PUFFER to port of axis along which SEA OWL was proceeding at thirteen knots speed of advance en route to area. Concentrated daily for radar tracking and communications.

Sent SEA OWL serial one informing O.T.C. 17.7 of our positions - barely within our submarine notice - and cruising disposition. Also warned other boats to remain on or ahead of schedule in view of possible confusion of submarine notice.

February 14

1435 IAfter radar tracking exercise, PUFFER reported appendicitis case on board. Directed her to arrange through O.T.C. 17.7 for rendezvous with ARCHERFISH to effect transfer, and detached her from formation to effect this.

A study of the new area brought out the following considerations governing patrol there:

(1) Assumption that 25-fathom restriction still applies, reduces considerably the available patrol area in Northern and Northwestern parts.

(2) We can expect the "plague of junks" to be at least as bad as in HONG KONG vicinity.

(3) Analysis of aircraft contacts for past month shows the principal routes are through HAINAN CHANNEL thence hugging CHINA coast, and cutting across from Southern end of HAINAN to HONG KONG. On the latter route, practically all contacts were North bound, most of them at night and high speed.

4. Narrow and varying fuel margins of BLAZERS would preclude coordinated surface patrol day and night. Presence of junks would probably hamper day-surface patrol, but small size of area would make concentration for scouting line each night to cover probable high speed routes.

Accordingly a patrol plan was issued, setting up four sub-areas for day time independent patrol, viz: (a) South of 19-30 N; (b) 19-30 N to 20-00 N; (c) North of 20-00 N and East of 113-30 E. A standard scouting line was ordered to originate with stations at fifteen mile intervals bearing 125° true from initial point 20-25 N; 111-55 E, and to advance ten knots on course 215° T from 2000 H each night. On surfacing each boat was to proceed to position on scouting line corresponding to area assignment, and likewise break away each morning in time to reach next day's diving point at best practicable speed,— all boats striving to maintain line at least from 2300 to 0300 H. Since eight days were left, assignments were to be rotated every other night.

CONFIDENTIAL

WEIGHT OF COORDINATED ATTACK GROUP 17.1A

10 April

SEA CAT, patrolling off WAKE, sighted a sampan type patrol craft close to the island. This craft was sighted every day but was never sufficiently clear of shore batteries to warrant riskin an attack on him.

16 April

SEA CAT made SJ contact 6 miles Northwest of WAKE on what was at first presumed to be the patrol craft, but was later identified as an enemy submarine when it dived during SEA CAT's surface approach.

On the assumption that this submarine would contact - or had contacted - the island and would return to the Empire, called in all BLAZERS for station patrol blocking probable retirement routes and SEA CAT commenced a close watch on the anchorage at WAKE (See SEA CAT track chart).

17 April

0029 L SEA CAT again contacted enemy submarine running 1 JACKPOT POINT close aboard and heading up for the anchorage. Again the enemy frustrated SEA CAT's attack by diving.

18 April

0446 L SEA CAT sunk enemy sub after contacting him third time anchored about five hundred yards off the boat landing. One torpedo of a depth and diver set spread hit the submarine aft and it sunk stern first. The other two torpedoes did not explode and are presumed to have been stopped by a torpedo net which was later seen.

The submarine was a very large one with no deck gun and is tentatively identified as an I-54 Class supply submarine (YUSEN). SEA CAT remained in the vicinity for an hour watching a landing barge and ex-USN motor launch pick up some seventy or eighty survivors, but was prevented from surfacing by the shore batteries on WAKE. Although certainly detected by the rescue craft, SEA CAT encountered no anti-submarine measures whatsoever, and it seems very probable that the patrol craft seen daily heretofore had been alongside the submarine and was sunk with it.

After pulling clear out of gun range, SEA CAT surfaced and reported sinking to remainder of pack and to COMSUBPAC. As all boats were probably putting pretty low on food and the probability of more targets in the immediate future was practically nil, all boats were ordered to discontinue patrol and proceed to their refit bases. DEAD-bound TRIGGFISH and PARAINITO were released from pack and a rendezvous was ordered for the original BLAZERS in order to proceed to MIDWAY in company.

CONFIDENTIAL

REPORT OF COORDINATED ATTACK GROUP 17,14

21-B April

0313BLAZERS arrived MIDWAY and commenced refit, whereupon the Coordinated Attack Group is considered disbanded.

(V) REMARKS

1. Interpack communications were extremely satisfactory, although the changing character of the patrol and the impossibility of doing much advance planning before departure made an excessive amount of transmissions necessary. Since all boats had ECM, that channel was used almost exclusively in promulgating patrol plans and area assignments,— the use of the ROMEO Code for these purposes is extremely awkward and unsatisfactory. Frequent conferences were held by VHF and were conducted with a full realization of the insecurity of this channel.

2. Communications with PHILIPPINES-based aircraft were very unsatisfactory at first but improved rapidly during the patrol. In several cases we failed to get reports of downed aviators until 12-24 hours after the ditching,— the intelligence having come via PHILIPPINES-COMSUPAC-NPM FOX, whereas we had a submarine on lifeguard duty nearby as well as one or more others usually also guarding that frequency with spare receivers. We cannot escape the conviction that had the planes communicated directly with us at the time and given us full and complete information at least some of these searches would have been successful. Happily this situation was well on the way to being cleared up before we left the area.

3. Communications with aircraft could have been immensely improved if we had access to their frequency plans and calls used. We were given calls for specific strikes, but friendly planes were with us almost constantly in addition to these strikes. PIRANHA accidentally intercepted transmissions from and established contact with search planes on 2274 kc. and this proved to be a useful channel. The lifeguard frequency at first was so cluttered with routine administrative and operational traffic that it was essentially useless for its primary purpose, but this situation too was showing rapid improvement.

4. Four definite and other possible encounters with enemy submarines or torpedo-firing small craft emphasizes the enhanced danger from that source as our aviators are driving the surface anti-submarine craft out of the "outer" areas.

5. The almost universal tendency of our night flying aircraft to come directly in on a b earing run made the patrol almost as unpleasant as the JAPS could have, and furthermore its purpose is not understood. Presumably they will not attack an unidentified target in a submarine patrol zone, so apparently they make this approach to see if the contact will dive. But usually, even if the contact did not dive! On the whole there is a crying need for a clean-cut and relatively enforced operating policy for these "shared" areas that will relieve the submarine of the rather gruelling necessity of treating our extensive night air search as enemy.

CONFIDENTIAL

REPORT OF COORDINATED ATTACK GROUP 17.14

6. The intelligent and cheerful spirit of cooperation manifested by the PUFFER and PILOTFISH throughout the patrol and by the THRESHER and RAZORBACK while they were attached was superb and made the Group Commander's Task an easy and a pleasant one. It was a source of keen disappointment that no opportunity was offered for carrying this cooperation to its supreme test in a coordinated attack. Although the maximum-up of the Group made it possible for the SEA OWL to hunt down and successfully attack the submarine encountered off MUKO, that type of "coordinated attack" offers little in the way of compensation to the boats that had to sit out in left field and wear a groove in the open ocean.
